direct: Pei et al. 2017 support a short, relatively deep, subtriangular skull with length-to-depth near 2.5:1, a large orbit, elongated naris, small teeth, a small body, and long lower legs.
Dingus et al. 2008 support eolian dunes, interdune settings, and episodic wet depositional contexts at Ukhaa Tolgod.
comparativeOrInferred: Living hand and toe form, complete distal tail, short feather covering, and the exact external body outline use close-troodontid comparison.
The distant unidentified ceratopsian-like animal in S5 is regional visual context only and is not identified to species.
hypothetical: Color, feather distribution, exact co-occurrence, vigilance, turning, and avoidance behavior are reconstruction hypotheses.
Loope et al. 1999 provide a depositional hypothesis for rain-related dune-slope collapse; the S6 animal's response is not fossil evidence.

promptLines: Asset type: Dino Atlas gallery slide, anatomy-review candidate

Primary request: Create a new naturalistic paleoart scene of one Almas ukhaa noticing a small fresh sand-slope slump after rain and turning away at a safe distance. This is a hypothetical vigilance/avoidance reconstruction, not evidence of observed behavior.

Input images: Image 1 is the approved project-owned Almas identity and anatomy reference, not an edit target. Preserve its species identity, body proportions, olive-brown and warm sand palette, pale throat, subtle blue-gray eye ring, and unbanded tail.

Scene/backdrop: Late Cretaceous Ukhaa Tolgod, Djadokhta-equivalent semiarid eolian dunes; damp interdune sand after a shower; one small localized trickle of fresh sand on a low dune face several body lengths away; no burial, no injury, no violent sandstorm.

Subject: exactly one small feathered Almas ukhaa in full body, shallow three-quarter side view, calmly but alertly changing direction away from the fresh sand movement. Skull length-to-depth about 2.5:1: short, relatively deep, subtriangular, with a large natural orbit, elongated naris, and small teeth in a non-bird jaw. Small light body, long lower legs, exactly two clearly separated forelimbs, exactly two hind limbs and exactly two feet, and exactly one continuous tail emerging from the pelvis.
Style/medium: museum-quality naturalistic scientific paleoart, anatomy-led, realistic feather and sand textures, restrained educational tone, no cartoon styling.

Composition/framing: landscape; the entire animal, both forelimbs, both hind limbs, both feet, pelvis-to-tail connection, and complete tail tip must remain visible and separated. Keep the minor sand slump readable but clearly distant from the animal.
Lighting/mood: soft post-rain daylight, damp sand highlights, quiet caution rather than disaster.

Constraints: no text, labels, logo, or watermark. No other animal, predator, prey, pack, family, nest, eggs, attack, injury, blood, chase, or direct-contact behavior. Do not imply this behavior is fossil evidence. Feather extent, color, and behavior remain comparative reconstruction.

Avoid: a long low Byronosaurus-like head, round owl face, modern bird beak, robust Zanabazar proportions, dromaeosaur body, flight wings or large arm-feather fans, regular tail rings, exaggerated sickle claw, hidden or fused feet, cropped or split tail, duplicated limb, third leg, extra foot, extra tail, malformed toes.

review.method: Original-size inspection of skull proportion, natural orbit, naris and tooth line, both separated forelimbs, both hind limbs and feet, pelvis-tail join, full tail tip, absence of duplicated anatomy, and safe spatial separation from the minor sand slump.
review.result: Approved only as the S6 defense anatomy-review image. One animal with two forelimbs, two hind limbs and feet, and one continuous unbanded tail passes. The pose and dune-slope response remain hypothetical and are not promoted as fossil behavior.
